I am a 49-year-old farmer in Quzhou County. I have been farming these lands for 20 years — my father taught me, and after primary school I came home to work the fields. I know my 9 mu like the back of my hand. My household has four people: my wife, my son, my daughter-in-law, and me. My son and daughter-in-law both work off-farm at a factory in Handan, so they send money home, but during busy times like cotton picking they come back to help. That means I am the one making the day-to-day decisions in the field.

**Cotton** is my main crop and my main cash income. I always put the biggest share of my land into cotton because it pays the bills, even though it is heavy work. This year I will plant 5 mu of cotton in late April. I use an improved variety — Guoxinmian or something similar from the seed shop in town — because the yield is better than the old local types and the fiber quality gets a good price at the coop. I rotary-till the soil before planting to break up the clods and keep moisture. For fertilizer, I put down one big bag of compound fertilizer per mu at planting, and I topdress with urea when the plants start flowering. After 20 years I know cotton is greedy — it needs plenty of food. I have a well, so I can irrigate three times: once after sowing, once at flowering, and once when the bolls are filling. I also know I must spray often — cotton bollworm and aphids are ruthless here. I count on about 15 sprays through the season, mixing insecticide, herbicide, and growth regulator as needed. I expect about 275 kg per mu if the weather cooperates.

**Maize** I plant on 3 mu as my summer crop, sown right after I clear the wheat stubble or on the land I rotate out of other crops. I buy hybrid seed packages — Denghai or Nongda — because hybrid maize outyields saved seed by a lot, and everyone around here knows it. I do no-tillage planting for summer maize; there is no time to plow deep in June, and the roots do fine if I just open a furrow and put the seed and fertilizer down together. I give it compound fertilizer at planting and that is usually enough. Two waterings from the well will carry it through — once after emergence and once at tasseling if the rains fail. Maize does not need much spraying, maybe three times total: herbicide once and insecticide once or twice. I expect around 500 kg per mu.

**Mungbean** I grow on 1 mu, partly because my wife likes to have some mungbean for home cooking and summer soup, and partly because it is a quick crop I can harvest by July before the heavy cotton picking starts. I use my own saved seed — traditional seed — because mungbean is simple and I do not need to buy new seed every year. I prepare that small plot with the rotary tiller when I do the cotton ground. I put down a modest amount of compound fertilizer, not too much because mungbean fixes some nitrogen on its own. Two waterings and maybe two sprays are all it needs. I expect about 65 kg per mu.

My neighbors sometimes ask why I do not grow more maize and less cotton. I tell them: cotton is what brings the cash to pay for my son's wedding expenses and the house repairs. Maize is steady but the price is low. Mungbean is just a side dish. With my well and my experience, I know how to manage these three crops through the year without hiring too much outside labor.
